newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems say Serb mortar bombs drove them from village.
newsitem.headline: Moslems say Serb mortar bombs drove them from village.

text.p: Bosnian Serb troops and police used mortars to drove Moslems out of the disputed village of Gajevi in one of the worst incidents of violence since the end of the Bosnian war, eyewitnesses said on Tuesday.
They told reporters in the nearby town of Celic in northeast Bosnia that two Moslem men were injured, one with a serious head wound, during the three hour attack.
The witnesses said up to 300 Serbs began the assault with mortars, rocket propelled grenades and small arms fire at 7 a.m. and alleged that Russian peacekeeping troops stood by without intervening.
Dr Ernad Alagic, who was among the men who fled said: "We saw the Serbs regrouping. We were completely encircled by them. What we saw was about 300 Serbs wearing police and army uniforms."
Another eyewitness, Semir Tukic, said: "Mortar bombs started to fall and we began to run down the hill. Two Russian APC's stopped us and asked to see whether we had weapons."

NATO peacekeepers reported earlier that shooting and explosions were heard around the village, in Serb territory which Moslems are trying to repopulate, but could not confirm Moslem claims that they were under attack by Serbs.
Around 600 Moslems, including women and children, were in Gajevi on Monday but it was not known how many had stayed overnight.
The witnesses said no Moslems were left in the village after the attack on Tuesday morning.
A spokesman for NATO-led peace forces in Bosnia, Major Brett Boudreau, acknowledged reports of shots and explosions but could not confirm that Serbs were attacking.
"The situation is fluid and there is evidence to suggest that there is sporadic fire going on. We are taking action to restore calm in the area," Boudreau told Reuters in Sarajevo.
"We are not necessarily saying that it is Serbs attacking Moslems. That does not jibe with the information we have."
Boudreau said NATO had no forces in the village but that there was, at a minimum, a Russian company and some U.S. forces in the area as well as U.S. Apache helicopters circling above.
"We are deploying an additional number of U.S. troops into the area," Boudreau said.
A spokeswoman at NATO's Task Force Eagle base in Tuzla said a Quick Reaction Force had been deployed into the Gajevi area on Tuesday morning once gunfire was reported.

She explained that communications were so poor in the area that members of the quick reaction team might have to return to Tuzla before a reliable account of what's happening on the ground would be available.

As many as 600 Moslems crossed the Inter-Entity Boundary Line (IEBL) northeast of Tuzla on Monday in an attempt to return to homes in Gajevi and Koraj, on Serb-administered territory, from which they were driven during the Bosnian war.
Some shots were fired on Monday and at least one Serb was reported to have been wounded. An unarmed U.N. police monitor was also wounded when a Serb policeman's handgun discharged accidentally.
Under the Dayton peace accord which ended the Bosnian war one year ago, the IEBL is supposed to be an administrative boundary line between Moslem-Croat and Serb territory.
Instead it has hardened into a de facto border across which refugees have been unable to return to homes located in areas controlled by rival communities.
